z-m-32-01.title: Given three points, is the fourth vertex the only one?
z-m-32-01.topic: The fourth vertex of a parallelogram (finding it with coordinates)
z-m-32-01.goal: Use coordinates to check that, for a parallelogram with three given points, there can be several fourth vertices depending on which point it is opposite to, and explain what changes when the three points lie on one line.
z-m-32-01.material: On a coordinate plane there are three points A(0, 0), B(4, 1), C(1, 3). You want to make a parallelogram that has these three points and one more point D as vertices. The order of the vertex names is not fixed. That is, D may be opposite to any of A, B, or C. Hayun found D=(5, 4) and said, "This is the only possible fourth point." (A parallelogram is a figure whose four points are not all on one line. One square of the grid has the same length in every direction.)
z-m-32-01.thinking.0: Checking the first judgment (the claim "the only one")
z-m-32-01.thinking.1: Building several solutions inside the constraints yourself
z-m-32-01.thinking.2: Finding the condition for it to work (the three points are not on one line)
z-m-32-01.prereq.0: Middle school geometry: the definition and properties of a parallelogram
z-m-32-01.prereq.1: Reading the coordinates of points on a coordinate plane, and adding and subtracting coordinates
z-m-32-01.prereq.2: Assumed school sequence: assumes the learner has finished middle school math (linear functions, the Pythagorean theorem, properties of figures) and has just started the equations of figures unit of high school Common Mathematics. 'H1' is only a label for the difficulty and support level of this production assignment, not a grade placement in the curriculum.
z-m-32-01.s.s1.prompt: When you first read Hayun's statement, how do you judge it? Choose the one closest to what you think now. (It's okay to be wrong. You will test it yourself in the steps below.)
z-m-32-01.s.s1.hint.0: Plot A, B, and C as points on a coordinate plane and join the three points to draw a triangle.
z-m-32-01.s.s1.r.a: This judgment assumes that once three points are fixed, the last point is fixed too. But did the problem say which point D is opposite to?
z-m-32-01.s.s1.explain: If the three points are not on one line, the case where D is opposite A, the case where it is opposite B, and the case where it is opposite C each make one parallelogram, so there are 3. (5, 4) is one of them. In the next step you will build them yourself to check.
z-m-32-01.s.s2.prompt: Enter 3 different coordinates (x, y) for D. Only points that make a parallelogram together with A, B, and C are accepted. (Hayun's (5, 4) counts as one of them.)
z-m-32-01.s.s2.hint.1: Observe how the two segments joining opposite vertices are related to each other, and turn that relationship into a calculation with coordinates.
z-m-32-01.s.s2.ok.c1: This makes a parallelogram in which D is opposite one of A, B, and C.
z-m-32-01.s.s2.fail.c1: This point does not make a parallelogram. Look at the shape of the two segments joining the pairs of opposite vertices.
z-m-32-01.s.s2.explain: If D is opposite A it is (5, 4), if opposite B it is (−3, 2), and if opposite C it is (3, −2). In all three cases, the two segments joining the two pairs of opposite vertices meet at each other's midpoints.
z-m-32-01.s.s3.prompt: If the three points are on one line, like A(0, 0), P(1, 1), Q(2, 2), how many possible points are there for D? Write the number and the reason in one or two sentences.
z-m-32-01.s.s3.hint.0: Plot A, P, and Q on a coordinate plane and see whether these three points form a triangle.
z-m-32-01.s.s3.hint.1: Sketch what shape the four points make when D is on the line and when D is off the line.
z-m-32-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Are both the 'number' and the 'reason' clear in my answer?
z-m-32-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I connect the fact that the three points do not form a triangle to the conclusion that no parallelogram is possible?
z-m-32-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I consider both the case where D is on the line and the case where D is off the line?
z-m-32-01.s.s3.model.0: If three points are on one line, no matter where you put D you can't make a parallelogram. The three points have to form a triangle for the 3 cases, changing the opposite point, to appear.
z-m-32-01.s.s3.model.1: A, P, and Q are in a straight line, so no triangle forms, and whether D is on the line or off it, no parallelogram forms, so the number is 0.
z-m-32-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: It is good that you split D into on the line and off the line.

z-m-32-02.title: Does the rule 'multiply the slopes to get −1' explain everything about perpendicular lines?
z-m-32-02.topic: Perpendicular lines and the product of their slopes
z-m-32-02.goal: Use examples to check that the rule 'if lines are perpendicular, the product of their slopes is −1' is used only when both lines have slopes, and compare ways of checking that also cover lines with no slope.
z-m-32-02.material: Minseo summarized it like this: "If two lines are perpendicular, the product of their slopes is −1. So if the product is not −1, they are not perpendicular." Doyun asked, "Then the vertical line x=2 and the horizontal line y=3 can't have their slopes multiplied, so they aren't perpendicular, right?" Assume every line extends straight and endlessly in both directions, and the units on the coordinate axes are the same. (x=2 is the line where the value of x is always 2, a vertical line parallel to the y-axis. y=3 is a horizontal line parallel to the x-axis.)
z-m-32-02.thinking.0: Finding the range (condition) where the rule holds
z-m-32-02.thinking.1: Revising a belief as examples pile up
z-m-32-02.prereq.0: The meaning of slope for a line y=mx+n (middle school linear functions)
z-m-32-02.prereq.1: Has already learned once the perpendicularity condition 'if two lines are perpendicular, the product of their slopes is −1'
z-m-32-02.prereq.2: Assumed school sequence: assumes the learner has finished middle school math (linear functions, the Pythagorean theorem, properties of figures) and has just started the equations of figures unit of high school Common Mathematics. 'H1' is only a label for the difficulty and support level of this production assignment, not a grade placement in the curriculum.
z-m-32-02.s.s1.prompt: As each example is revealed, choose a judgment about how Minseo's rule applies.
z-m-32-02.s.s1.hint.0: In each example, first check whether both lines have slopes.
z-m-32-02.s.s1.hint.1: Sort the examples into those where the rule works and those where it is hard to judge by the rule, and write them in a table.
z-m-32-02.s.s1.st.0.info: Line l: y=3x−1, line m: y=−(1/3)x+2 (the slope of m is minus one third).
z-m-32-02.s.s1.st.0.after: The product of the slopes is 3×(−1/3)=−1, so by Minseo's rule they are perpendicular.
z-m-32-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This may be a judgment based only on seeing that the slopes are different. To know whether lines are perpendicular, you need to look at how the slopes are related to each other.
z-m-32-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This judgment looks at how the two slopes are related. Can you state the reason you applied the rule to this case?
z-m-32-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: You can't tell without a picture
z-m-32-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Think about whether there is a rule you can use to judge from the information in the equations, even without a picture.
z-m-32-02.s.s1.st.1.info: Consider line l: x=2 (a vertical line) and line m: y=3 (a horizontal line).
z-m-32-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: Are these two lines perpendicular? What happens to Minseo's rule?
z-m-32-02.s.s1.st.1.after: A vertical line and a horizontal line meet at a right angle, so they are perpendicular. But a vertical line has no slope, so you can't check it with the rule 'the product is −1'. Minseo's rule needs the condition 'when both lines have slopes'.
z-m-32-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Not perpendicular. You can't multiply the slopes, so the product can't be −1
z-m-32-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This judgment turns 'the rule's result is not −1' into 'not perpendicular'. First work out whether these are lines the rule can be used on.
z-m-32-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: You can't decide whether they are perpendicular. Without a slope you can't judge
z-m-32-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Not being able to use a rule is different from not being able to judge. The angle that a vertical line and a horizontal line make can be examined another way.
z-m-32-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Perpendicular. But a vertical line has no slope, so you can't check it with the product rule
z-m-32-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This judgment thinks separately about the limit of the rule and about the angle the two lines make.
z-m-32-02.s.s1.st.2.info: Line l: 3x+4y−5=0, line m: 4x−3y+7=0. (The coefficients of x are 3 and 4, and the coefficients of y are 4 and −3.)
z-m-32-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: Choose one valid way to check whether the two lines are perpendicular.
z-m-32-02.s.s1.st.2.after: In method a the slopes are −3/4 and 4/3 and their product is −1, so they are perpendicular. In method c, 3×4+4×(−3)=0, so they are also perpendicular. Method c can also be used as it is for x=2 (1x+0y−2=0) and y=3 (0x+1y−3=0), since 1×0+0×1=0. In method b, 3×4=12 is not a product of slopes, so it is not a valid reason.
z-m-32-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Rewrite both equations in the form y=mx+n, find the slopes, and multiply them
z-m-32-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This is a method you use after checking the rule's condition (both lines have slopes).
z-m-32-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Check whether the product of the coefficients of x is −1
z-m-32-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You may have missed that the rule is about slopes. Is the slope the same value as the coefficient of x?
z-m-32-02.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Add the product of the coefficients of x and the product of the coefficients of y, and check whether it is 0
z-m-32-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This is a method that tries to judge without finding the slopes. It is worth testing whether it also works for lines like x=2 and y=3.
z-m-32-02.s.s1.reflect: After Doyun's question, how did your belief about Minseo's rule change? Did you throw the rule away, or did you attach a condition for when it can be used? What confidence does it give you that the two methods reached the same conclusion in step 3?
z-m-32-02.s.s2.prompt: Rewrite Minseo's statement in two or three sentences so that it can also explain Doyun's question. Also say which lines this rule can't be used on.
z-m-32-02.s.s2.hint.0: Look again at the equation of the line the rule couldn't be used on in step 2, and write that line's feature in a few words.
z-m-32-02.s.s2.hint.1: Write what condition needs to go in front of the sentence that begins 'If the product is −1'.
z-m-32-02.s.s2.placeholder: Example: When two lines are ..., if they are perpendicular then ...
z-m-32-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: In the corrected rule, did I distinguish 'if the product is −1, then perpendicular' from 'if perpendicular, then the product is −1'?
z-m-32-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did I clearly say in my answer whether x=2 and y=3 are perpendicular?
z-m-32-02.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did I state exactly, in my own words, the condition where the rule works?
z-m-32-02.s.s2.model.0: When both lines have slopes, if they are perpendicular the product of the slopes is −1, and if the product is −1 they are perpendicular. But a vertical line like x=2 has no slope, so you can't use this rule, and you have to treat separately that a vertical line and a horizontal line are perpendicular.
z-m-32-02.s.s2.model.1: It's true that if the product is −1 they are perpendicular. But there are cases where lines are perpendicular and the product can't be found, for example x=2 and y=3. A vertical line has no defined slope, so leave that case out of the rule and check it separately.
z-m-32-02.s.s2.modelNote.1: It states both the limit of the rule and the conclusion for that case (perpendicular).

z-m-32-03.title: The moved circle's equation looks wrong: where did it go off track?
z-m-32-03.goal: Find the error in a solution for the equation of a translated figure, where the direction of the move was applied the wrong way round, and tell apart the checks that can reveal the error from the checks that cannot.
z-m-32-03.material: Seoyun solved for the equation of the circle C: (x+1)²+(y−2)²=9 moved by +3 in the x direction and −4 in the y direction, as shown below. (+3 in the x direction means 3 units to the right, and −4 in the y direction means 4 units down. The rule for moving one point is that (x, y) goes to (x+3, y−4). The equation of circle C is read as 'x plus 1 squared plus y minus 2 squared equals 9'.)
z-m-32-03.thinking.0: Finding the line where the error began in the solution
z-m-32-03.thinking.1: Comparing checks that reveal the error
z-m-32-03.thinking.2: Using the corrected equation to build movements that meet a condition
z-m-32-03.prereq.0: The meaning of the circle equation (x−a)²+(y−b)²=r² (center (a, b), radius r)
z-m-32-03.prereq.1: Moving a point (x, y) by p in the x direction and q in the y direction gives (x+p, y+q)
z-m-32-03.prereq.2: Assumed school sequence: assumes the learner has finished middle school math (linear functions, the Pythagorean theorem, properties of figures) and has just started the equations of figures unit of high school Common Mathematics. 'H1' is only a label for the difficulty and support level of this production assignment, not a grade placement in the curriculum.
z-m-32-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in Seoyun's solution that goes wrong.
z-m-32-03.s.s1.hint.0: Read each line and check, one line at a time, whether it follows naturally from the result of the line before.
z-m-32-03.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the point you get by moving the center of circle C by the problem's rule with the center in Seoyun's last line.
z-m-32-03.s.s1.line.0: Find the equation of the figure obtained by moving circle C by +3 in the x direction and −4 in the y direction.
z-m-32-03.s.s1.line.1: When a point (x, y) on the figure is moved, it becomes (x+3, y−4), so replace x with x+3 and y with y−4 in the equation.
z-m-32-03.s.s1.line.4: So it is a circle with center (−4, 6) and radius 3.
z-m-32-03.s.s1.explain: It went wrong at line 2. A point (X, Y) on the moved figure is a point (X−3, Y+4) of the original figure that has moved over, so X−3 and Y+4 should go in the places of x and y in the original equation. Seoyun's equation sends the center to (−4, 6), but moving the original center (−1, 2) by (+3, −4) gives (2, −2). To check: the point (−1, 5) on circle C moves to (2, 1), and putting this point into Seoyun's new equation gives 6²+(−5)²=61, not 9. Lines 3 to 5 just follow from the result of line 2.
z-m-32-03.s.s2.prompt: After Seoyun finishes the solution, which checks would be useful for noticing the error right away? Choose all the checks that can actually reveal the error in this solution.
z-m-32-03.s.s2.hint.0: Write down which value in Seoyun's new equation has not changed from the first equation.
z-m-32-03.s.s2.hint.1: Think about whether the error is about position or about size, and compare whether each check looks at that value.
z-m-32-03.s.s2.o.a: Check whether the right side of the new equation is still 9 and the radius is still 3
z-m-32-03.s.s2.r.a: In this solution the radius is the same as before, so this check alone does not reveal the error. Think about whether this check looks at the shape of the figure or its position.
z-m-32-03.s.s2.o.b: Move the center of circle C by the same rule and compare it with the center in the new equation
z-m-32-03.s.s2.r.b: This idea is to calculate the position after the move directly with the movement rule and compare.
z-m-32-03.s.s2.o.c: Expand the new equation and check whether the coefficients of x² and y² are both still 1
z-m-32-03.s.s2.r.c: The coefficients do not change under a translation, so they stay the same even in the wrong solution. This check does not look at the direction or size of the move.
z-m-32-03.s.s2.o.d: Move one point on circle C by the same rule and put it into the new equation to see whether it fits
z-m-32-03.s.s2.r.d: This idea is to directly test whether the point that a point of the original figure moves to satisfies the new equation.
z-m-32-03.s.s2.explain: Seoyun's new equation has the same radius and the same coefficients of x² and y² as before, so checks a and c pass. The error is in the 'position after the move', so checks b and d, which move the center or a point on the figure by the same rule and compare with the new equation, reveal the error.
z-m-32-03.s.s3.prompt: You moved circle C by p in the x direction and q in the y direction (the radius stays 3 after moving), and it became a circle passing through the origin (0, 0). Enter 3 different possible (p, q). (Decimals are fine.)
z-m-32-03.s.s3.hint.0: First write the new center, which is the center (−1, 2) of circle C moved by p and q, in terms of p and q.
z-m-32-03.s.s3.hint.1: Apply to the new center and the origin the fact that every point on a circle is at a fixed distance from the center.
z-m-32-03.s.s3.var.p: Movement in the x direction, p
z-m-32-03.s.s3.var.q: Movement in the y direction, q
z-m-32-03.s.s3.ok.c1: The moved circle passes through the origin.
z-m-32-03.s.s3.fail.c1: The moved circle does not pass through the origin. Write the new center in terms of p and q and check the distance to the origin.
z-m-32-03.s.s3.explain: The new center is (−1+p, 2+q), and for the origin to be on the circle, the distance between the origin and the new center must be the radius 3. That is, (p−1)²+(q+2)²=9. The integer solutions are (4, −2), (−2, −2), (1, 1), (1, −5), and there are also decimal solutions. For the movement (3, −4) in the original problem, the new center is (2, −2), and its distance from the origin is √8, so the circle does not pass through the origin.

z-m-32-04.title: Is the information 'they touch at only one point' enough?
z-m-32-04.topic: The position of two circles and the distance between their centers
z-m-32-04.goal: Learn that the information that two circles meet at one point does not fix the distance between the centers to a single value, say what further information is needed, and explain the range of distances for which they meet at two points.
z-m-32-04.material: Circular flower bed A has its center at the origin O(0, 0) and radius 3 (unit: m). As an equation, it is x²+y²=9. Flower bed B is a circle with radius 5 (unit: m), and the position of its center has not been decided yet. The plan only says 'the boundary lines of the two flower beds meet at only one point'. Jion said, "They touch at only one point, so the distance d between the two centers is 3+5=8." (Think of a boundary as a line with no thickness. If the two circles are apart, or if one circle lies completely inside the other, their boundary lines do not meet.)
z-m-32-04.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough and saying what is missing
z-m-32-04.thinking.1: Building different types that meet the condition yourself
z-m-32-04.thinking.2: Explaining the range of distances (a conditional conclusion)
z-m-32-04.prereq.0: The circle equation x²+y²=r² and the distance between two points
z-m-32-04.prereq.1: The meaning that the distance between a point on a circle and the center is the radius
z-m-32-04.prereq.2: Assumed school sequence: assumes the learner has finished middle school math (linear functions, the Pythagorean theorem, properties of figures) and has just started the equations of figures unit of high school Common Mathematics. 'H1' is only a label for the difficulty and support level of this production assignment, not a grade placement in the curriculum.
z-m-32-04.s.s1.prompt: Can the information 'the boundary lines meet at only one point' fix d to a single value? Choose the most suitable judgment.
z-m-32-04.s.s1.hint.0: Draw a circle of radius 3, then draw one picture with a circle of radius 5 touching it from the outside and another with it touching from the inside.
z-m-32-04.s.s1.hint.1: In each picture, write the lengths and compare how the distance between the two centers is related to the two radii.
z-m-32-04.s.s1.r.c: This judgment only pictured the case where the small circle touches the big circle from the inside. Circles touching from the outside also meet at one point.
z-m-32-04.s.s1.o.d: More information is needed, so you can't state the value of d
z-m-32-04.s.s1.r.d: The judgment that more is needed is valid. But think about whether you can also say what information is needed and, depending on it, which of how many values d will be.
z-m-32-04.s.s1.explain: There are two cases where two circles meet at only one point. If they touch from the outside, d=3+5=8, and if the small circle A touches the inside of the big circle B, d=5−3=2. So you need to know more about 'which way they touch' for d to be fixed to one value.
z-m-32-04.s.s1.acc.0: The conclusion that the information is not enough is right. Going one step further, if you know 'whether they touch from the outside or from the inside', d is fixed to either 8 or 2.
z-m-32-04.s.s2.prompt: Decide the center (x, y) of flower bed B and make a layout where the two boundary lines meet at only one point. You are done when you enter two layouts whose distances from the origin to the center of B are different.
z-m-32-04.s.s2.hint.0: Write the square of the distance from the origin to the center in terms of x and y.
z-m-32-04.s.s2.hint.1: First decide the distance for each of the two cases where they meet at one point, then pick one point for each distance.
z-m-32-04.s.s2.var.x: x-coordinate of the center of B
z-m-32-04.s.s2.var.y: y-coordinate of the center of B
z-m-32-04.s.s2.ok.c1: The two boundary lines meet at only one point.
z-m-32-04.s.s2.fail.c1: With this center, the two boundary lines do not meet at one point (they do not meet, or they meet at two points). Compare the distance from the origin to the center with the two radii.
z-m-32-04.s.s2.explain: If the distance from the origin to the center is 8, they touch from the outside (e.g. (8, 0)), and if it is 2, they touch from the inside (e.g. (0, 2)). If the distances are equal (e.g. (8, 0) and (0, 8)), they are the same type of layout, so count them as one.
z-m-32-04.s.s3.prompt: Imagine increasing d gradually from 0. Write the range of d for which the two boundary lines meet at two different points, and explain why it is that range using one method. (Explain in words instead of a picture.)
z-m-32-04.s.s3.hint.0: Using the distances of the two layouts you made in step 2 as references, sketch how the two circles lie at distances between them and at distances outside them.
z-m-32-04.s.s3.hint.1: Check separately whether the two circles touch when d is less than 2 and when d is greater than 8.
z-m-32-04.s.s3.placeholder: Example: When d is ..., they meet at two points. Because ...
z-m-32-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did I say that the two ends of the range where they meet at two points (d=2, d=8) are not included?
z-m-32-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I explain what the two boundary lines look like when d is less than 2 and when d is greater than 8?
z-m-32-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Can the reason I wrote get across to a reader even without a picture?
z-m-32-04.s.s3.model.0: When 2<d<8, they meet at two points. If d=2 they touch at one point from the inside, and if d=8 they touch at one point from the outside, so in between, the two circles overlap as if crossing each other and meet at two points.
z-m-32-04.s.s3.model.1: It is when d is greater than the difference of the two radii, 5−3=2, and less than their sum, 3+5=8. If d is greater than the sum, they are apart, and if it is less than the difference, the small circle is inside the big circle, so they do not meet.
z-m-32-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: It explains the boundary values using the difference and the sum of the radii.

z-m-32-05.title: On a road, is there only one spot where the ratio of the distances is 2:1?
z-m-32-05.topic: Interior and exterior division points of a segment: a point with a fixed ratio of distances
z-m-32-05.goal: Check that on a line, points whose distances to two points have a fixed ratio can be on the inside or the outside, and explain how the number of such points changes when you restrict to a segment or when the ratio becomes 1:1.
z-m-32-05.material: On a coordinate plane, think of one grid square as 1 km. Assume the straight road goes on endlessly in both directions, and on the road there are two towns A(0, 0) and B(6, 3). You want to put up a relay tower P on this road so that its distance to A is 2 times its distance to B. That is, PA:PB=2:1. Soyun said, "It's the point that divides segment AB in the ratio 2:1, so it's just one point, (4, 2)."
z-m-32-05.thinking.0: Checking the first judgment (only one spot)
z-m-32-05.thinking.1: Finding several points that meet the condition yourself
z-m-32-05.thinking.2: Explaining how the count changes when the condition changes
z-m-32-05.prereq.0: The distance between two points and the Pythagorean theorem
z-m-32-05.prereq.1: Expressing a point on a line with coordinates (middle school linear functions)
z-m-32-05.prereq.2: Assumed school sequence: assumes the learner has finished middle school math (linear functions, the Pythagorean theorem, properties of figures) and has just started the equations of figures unit of high school Common Mathematics. 'H1' is only a label for the difficulty and support level of this production assignment, not a grade placement in the curriculum.
z-m-32-05.s.s1.prompt: Read Soyun's statement and choose your current judgment. How many spots on the road meet the condition for P?
z-m-32-05.s.s1.hint.0: Divide the road into three parts, 'outside A', 'between the two towns', and 'outside B', and in each part compare which of PA and PB is longer.
z-m-32-05.s.s1.hint.1: In each part, move P little by little and observe how PA÷PB changes.
z-m-32-05.s.s1.r.a: This judgment just accepted Soyun's statement as it is. Check whether it took into account that the road is not a segment but a line that goes on endlessly in both directions.
z-m-32-05.s.s1.o.b: 3 spots in all (outside A, between the two towns, outside B)
z-m-32-05.s.s1.r.b: This judgment treated all three parts of the road as candidates. Compare which of PA and PB is longer in the part outside A.
z-m-32-05.s.s1.r.c: This judgment came from comparing PA and PB part by part along the road.
z-m-32-05.s.s1.o.d: You can't decide the number of spots from the coordinates alone
z-m-32-05.s.s1.r.d: All the coordinates are given, so you can examine the candidates and decide the number. You can judge by comparing the lengths part by part.
z-m-32-05.s.s1.explain: There is one spot between A and B and one spot outside B, so 2 spots in all. Outside A, B is always farther than A, so PA can never be 2 times PB.
z-m-32-05.s.s2.prompt: Enter 2 different points P(x, y) on the road that satisfy PA:PB=2:1.
z-m-32-05.s.s2.hint.0: Express a point on the road with one variable. For example, think about how many times the direction from A to B you need to go.
z-m-32-05.s.s2.hint.1: Shrink the road to a single number line with A at 0 and B at 3, find the positions where PA is 2 times PB, and then move them back to the original road.
z-m-32-05.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a point on line AB (the road).
z-m-32-05.s.s2.fail.c1: It is not a point on the road. Use the coordinates of A and B to find what relationship holds between the x-coordinate and y-coordinate of a point on the road.
z-m-32-05.s.s2.fail.c2: PA is not 2 times PB. Find each of the two distances and compare them.
z-m-32-05.s.s2.explain: Shrinking to a number line with A at 0 and B at 3, the points P with PA=2PB are 2 (between A and B) and 6 (outside B). Moving these back to coordinates on the road gives (4, 2) and (12, 6). (3, 1.5) is exactly in the middle of the two towns, so the ratio is 1:1, and for (−6, −3), PA:PB=1:2.
z-m-32-05.s.s3.prompt: If you restrict P to segment AB, how many spots are the candidates? And if you change the ratio to 1:1, how many spots are the candidates on the road (the line)? Write the number of spots together with the reason.

z-m-32-05.s.s3.model.1: Within the segment it is 1 spot. If the ratio is 1:1, it is only the midpoint of the two towns, 1 spot, and on the outside one town is always closer, so they can't be equal.

z-m-32-06.title: Can the lines drawn by changing k give every line through that point?
z-m-32-06.topic: The family of lines through a point, and the missing line
z-m-32-06.goal: Distinguish confidence gained from several examples from checking all cases, and use a counterexample to explain why the family of lines with parameter k does not contain every line through the point.
z-m-32-06.material: For each real value of k, one line l_k: kx−y+2k+1=0 is determined. (l_k is read 'l sub k', and the equation is read 'k times x minus y plus 2k plus 1 equals zero'. There is no picture.) Daeun drew the lines y=1, y=x+3, y=−x−1 for k=0, 1, −1, and all three lines passed through the point (−2, 1). Daeun said, "Every l_k passes through (−2, 1). So every line through (−2, 1) must be among the l_k."
z-m-32-06.thinking.0: Distinguishing adding more examples from checking all cases
z-m-32-06.thinking.1: Building the missing case (a counterexample) yourself
z-m-32-06.thinking.2: Explaining the limits of a way of expressing something
z-m-32-06.prereq.0: The meaning of the slope and y-intercept in the line equation y=mx+n
z-m-32-06.prereq.1: Putting a point's coordinates into an equation to check whether the point lies on the line
z-m-32-06.prereq.2: Assumed school sequence: assumes the learner has finished middle school math (linear functions, the Pythagorean theorem, properties of figures) and has just started the equations of figures unit of high school Common Mathematics. 'H1' is only a label for the difficulty and support level of this production assignment, not a grade placement in the curriculum.
z-m-32-06.s.s1.prompt: Daeun became sure that 'every l_k passes through (−2, 1)' after seeing only three lines. Which check would make this confidence the most trustworthy?
z-m-32-06.s.s1.hint.0: Compare whether 'it held three times' and 'it holds for every k' mean the same thing.
z-m-32-06.s.s1.hint.1: Predict whether putting in an odd value like 1000 for k would give the same result, and think about why.
z-m-32-06.s.s1.o.a: Put in k=2, k=3, and k=10 too, draw the lines, and see whether they all pass through the point
z-m-32-06.s.s1.r.a: More examples make you more confident. But you have not checked every real number that k can be.
z-m-32-06.s.s1.o.b: When k=0, the line y=1 passes through the point (−2, 1), so that is enough
z-m-32-06.s.s1.r.b: This judgment took something true for one value of k to be true for all k.
z-m-32-06.s.s1.o.c: Put the point (−2, 1) into the equation and see whether the equation holds no matter what the value of k is
z-m-32-06.s.s1.r.c: This idea is to check all values at once, keeping k as a letter.
z-m-32-06.s.s1.o.d: If the lines you drew look like they meet at one point, that is enough
z-m-32-06.s.s1.r.d: This judgment used how it looked to the eye as evidence. A picture makes it hard to tell a point that is very close from exactly the same point.
z-m-32-06.s.s1.explain: Putting the point (−2, 1) into the equation gives k×(−2)−1+2k+1=0, which holds no matter what k is. Collecting more examples raises your confidence, but the guarantee that it holds for every k comes from a check that keeps k as a letter.
z-m-32-06.s.s1.acc.0: Collecting more examples is a reasonable first step that builds confidence. But to get a guarantee for 'every k', you need one check that keeps k as a letter.
z-m-32-06.s.s2.prompt: Test Daeun's second idea, 'every line through (−2, 1) is some l_k'. Enter 3 different points (p, q) that do not lie on l_k for any real number k you choose.
z-m-32-06.s.s2.hint.0: Fix one point (p, q), put it into the equation, make an equation in which only k remains, and see whether k can be found.
z-m-32-06.s.s2.ok.c1: This is a point that does not lie on l_k whatever k you choose.
z-m-32-06.s.s2.fail.c1: This point lies on l_k if you choose the right k. Put the point's coordinates into the equation and treat it as an equation in k. When is it impossible to find k?
z-m-32-06.s.s2.explain: Putting the point (p, q) into the equation gives k(p+2)=q−1. If p=−2, the left side is 0 whatever k is, so it holds only when q=1, and if q≠1 it does not hold for any k. These points all lie on the line x=−2. (0, 3) is on l_1 when k=1, and (−2, 1) is on every l_k.
z-m-32-06.s.s3.prompt: Write what you would tell Daeun. (1) Which line passes through the point (−2, 1) but cannot be written as an l_k? (2) Why is such a line missing?
z-m-32-06.s.s3.hint.1: Rewrite l_k in the form y=(…) and observe what k determines.
z-m-32-06.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Among the lines through (−2, 1), ... is missing. Because ...
z-m-32-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did I write the missing line's equation (or shape) exactly?
z-m-32-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I explain what role k plays that makes that line missing?
z-m-32-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I point out that 'every l_k passes through (−2, 1)' and 'every line through (−2, 1) is an l_k' are different statements?
z-m-32-06.s.s3.model.0: The vertical line x=−2 is missing. l_k is y=k(x+2)+1, so k plays the role of the slope, and a vertical line has no slope, so no k can make it.
z-m-32-06.s.s3.model.1: The line x=−2, which passes through (−2, 1) but is parallel to the y-axis, doesn't come out for any k. This is because the form y−1=k(x+2) only represents lines that have a slope k.
z-m-32-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: This answer gives the form of the equation as the reason.
